Learning Objectives

cuff.

tourniquet use.

The first tourniquet dated from between 199 BCE and 500 CE and was made of bronze and
leather.
The term tourniquet was coined by Jean Louis Petit as a derivation of the French verb tourner,
meaning to turn.
Harvey Cushing introduced the first pneumatic (inflatable) tourniquet in 1904, allowing
pressure to be monitored and manually controlled.

History
The use of a tourniquet to achieve hemostasis is common in the prehospital trauma
setting1,2 and the clinical setting. For orthopaedic surgeons, tourniquets are an often
overlooked staple of daily life. The tourniquet is a useful aid for extremity surgery
because it decreases blood loss during a surgical procedure and provides a relatively
bloodless field to improve visualization. Although functioning to achieve the same goal of
hemostasis, current tourniquets are drastically different than their predecessors.
The earliest recorded usage of a tourniquet was between 199 BCE and 500 CE in the
Roman Empire to control bleeding from limb amputations that occurred during war.3
These early, nonpneumatic tourniquets were made of bronze and leather (Figure 1).
Centuries later, Jean Louis Petit coined the term tourniquet as a derivation of the French
verb tourner, meaning to turn. At the time, tourniquets were screw-like devices that
tightened a belt to stop arterial blood flow.4 By 1864, Joseph Lister advanced the use of a
tourniquet as a tool to create a bloodless surgical field,5 and by the end of the 1800s,
Fredrich von Esmarch had created a rubber bandage to exsanguinate the limb and stop
blood flow, further advancing tourniquet design and use.6 These early nonpneumatic
designs often generated extremely high pressures that were not standardized between
applications. In addition, large shearing forces were expected during the application of
these early tourniquets, leading to considerable skin trauma and pain. In 1904, Harvey
Cushing introduced the first pneumatic (inflatable) tourniquet, which allowed pressure
to be monitored and manually controlled.7 The modern pneumatic tourniquet system
has its origins in the original device described by Harvey Cushing.

Modern Pneumatic Tourniquet System and Cuff Design
The modern, microcomputer-controlled pneumatic tourniquet maintains cuff pressure within
1% of the set pressure.
Microprocessors ensure self-compensation, maintaining a constant preset cuff pressure
during limb movements and changes in limb size.
Actual levels of pressure applied by a pneumatic tourniquet cuff to the underlying limb and
soft tissues vary in comparison with the pneumatic inflation pressure within the tourniquet
cuff.
Closer to the cuff edges, tissue pressures decrease progressively approximately 90% from the
midpoint of the cuff width to the cuff edge.
An inverse relationship exists between limb occlusion pressure (LOP) and the ratio of the cuff
width to the limb circumference.
Narrower cuffs require higher tourniquet pressures to stop blood flow.

Contoured tourniquet cuffs occlude blood flow at lower inflation pressures than straight
(cylindric) cuffs of equivalent width.

Modern Pneumatic Tourniquet System and Cuff Design
Currently, the modern pneumatic tourniquet is used in an estimated 15,000 surgical
procedures daily in the United States and abroad. Improvements in tourniquet
technology have resulted in improved safety, efficacy, and reliability of pneumatic
tourniquets. The US FDA has classified the modern pneumatic tourniquet as a class I
medical device, indicating that it presents minimal harm to the user and does not
present a reasonable source of injury via normal use.3 The modern microcomputer-
based pneumatic tourniquet system, on which current systems originated, was designed
in 1981. Its elements are shown in Figure 2.
SEND FEEDBACK

Figure 2 Illustration shows a modern tourniquet system with elements that have
improved safety, accuracy, and reliability. Microprocessor technology allows for precise
sensing and regulation of the actual cuff pressure, enables accurate indications of cuff
pressure and elapsed time to be provided visually, produces automatic audiovisual
alarms in the event of a wide range of hazardous conditions, and allows for automatic
estimation of limb occlusion pressure (LOP). Improved cuff designs allows cuff pressure
to be applied effectively to encircled limbs with a wide range of sizes and shapes. IVRA =
intravenous regional anesthesia, OR = operating room. (Reproduced with permission
from McLaren, AC, Rorabeck CH: The pressure distribution under tourniquets. J Bone
Joint Surg Am 1985;67[3]:433-438.)
Knowledge of the basic mechanisms by which a modern pneumatic tourniquet functions
is critical for any extremity surgeon. A modern pneumatic tourniquet system consists of
several components to allow for safe and precise regulation of cuff pressure, which
minimizes excessive inflation or accidental deflation of the cuff intraoperatively. In most
systems, a microcomputer-controlled pressure regulator functions to maintain cuff
pressure within 1% of the set pressure. The microprocessor ensures self-compensation,
maintaining a constant preset cuff pressure during limb movements and changes in limb
size. This reliability in maintaining cuff pressure reduces variability and allows for lower
overall pressures to be used. Many modern tourniquets also have automatic timers to
provide a record of inflation time and avoid excessive durations.3 Automatic detection
and monitoring of potentially hazardous air leakage from the pressurized cuff often is
included, and self-test capabilities frequently are available to provide checks of
calibration, audiovisual alarms, and hardware and software integrity at each start-up of
the instrument. In addition, many tourniquets have a backup power source in the event
of unanticipated power interruptions. Modern tourniquet systems also include
additional safety features, such as a cuff hazard interlock, which prevents users from
inadvertently powering off a tourniquet if the cuff is inflated. Some tourniquets have an
intravenous regional anesthesia safety interlock to aid in preventing users from
inadvertently deflating the wrong cuff during intravenous regional anesthesia and
bilateral limb procedures. To facilitate the measurement of LOP, some modern
tourniquet systems also include a connection to physiologic monitors.

In addition to understanding the mechanics of a modern pneumatic tourniquet,
surgeons must comprehend cuff design before use. McLaren and Rorabeck8 studied the
influence of cuff design extensively. With regard to its function, the actual levels of
pressure applied by a pneumatic tourniquet cuff to the underlying limb and soft tissues
vary from the pneumatic inflation pressure within the tourniquet cuff. For example, in a
study of canine limbs, the peak pressure, which was 97% of the cuff inflation pressure,
was in the subcutaneous tissue just proximal to the mid-position along the tourniquet
width. Closer to the cuff edges, tissue pressures decrease progressively approximately
90% from the midpoint of the cuff width to the cuff edge. In addition, pressures are
lower in deeper tissues; however, this decrease from the limb surface to the center is
only approximately 2%. A decrease in tissue pressure with increasing depth also has
been demonstrated by Shaw and Murray,9 who noted the pressure measured in the soft
tissue was consistently lower than the pneumatic pressure in the tourniquet cuff and
that the level of tissue pressure varied inversely with thigh circumference. These studies
emphasize that higher tourniquet inflation pressures and higher applied pressure
gradients on the limb surface correspond with higher pressures and higher pressure
gradients in the underlying soft tissues.3
The distribution of perineural pressures under the cuff can be described by a parabolic
curve (Figure 3), with peak levels at the midpoint of the cuff and much lower pressures
at the proximal and distal edges.10 A direct relationship exists between the level of the
cuff inflation pressure and the pressure gradient in the underlying soft tissue, with the
difference between soft-tissue pressures at the cuff midpoint and those at the cuff edges
increasing at higher levels of cuff inflation. In addition, an inverse relationship exists
between LOP and the ratio of the cuff width to the limb circumference.11 For example,
for a given limb circumference, a narrower cuff requires a much higher tourniquet
pressure to stop blood flow. This is associated with higher applied pressure gradients
and a greater risk of neurologic injury. Conversely, for the same limb circumference, a
wider cuff requires a lower tourniquet pressure to stop blood flow. In addition, a
contoured tourniquet cuff has been found to occlude blood flow at a lower inflation
pressure than a straight (cylindrical) cuff of equivalent width;12 this is thought to be
because of better fit of the cuff to the limb and, therefore, more efficient transmission of
pressure to the underlying tissue. Therefore, extremity surgery has seen an increasing

use of wider, variable-contour cuffs that conform to a variety of limb shapes, stopping
blood flow at pressures lower than those necessary with narrower, cylindric cuffs.
Figure 3 Graph shows limb occlusion pressure (LOP) versus the ratio of tourniquet cuff
width (W) to limb circumference (C). For any given limb circumference, the tourniquet
pressure required to stop arterial blood flow decreases inversely as the width of the
tourniquet cuff increases. (Reproduced with permission from Graham B, Breault MJ,
McEwen JA, McGraw RW: Occlusion of arterial flow in the extremities at subsystolic
pressures through the use of wide tourniquet cuffs. Clin Orthop Relat Res 1993;286:257-
261.)
Pre-Application Precautions
Patient safety should be the primary consideration in selecting a pneumatic tourniquet and
accessories.
Relative contraindications to tourniquet use should be investigated before application.

A pneumatic tourniquet should be applied only by experienced personnel who are
knowledgeable about its use and potential complications.
Bruner’s 10 rules for safe use of a tourniquet may be a helpful guide (Table 1).13


Pre-Application Precautions
Before use of a tourniquet, the pressure source, cuff, regulator, tubing, and connectors
must be inspected, tested, and maintained according to the manufacturers’ written
instructions. The tourniquet and accessories should be cleaned after each use and kept
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:56 AM
AAOS | Tourniquets
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003021
8/33

in good condition by routinely checking all valves and gauges because inaccuracies may
result in excessively high inflation pressures, which may lead to complications. Specific
recommendations for maintenance include daily calibration checks, intraoperative
monitoring of tourniquet function at frequent intervals, and rigorous monthly
performance-assurance tests. These monthly tests involve determining if the actual
pressure is accurate to within 5% of the set pressure and remains stable to within 10% of
the set pressure over a 15-minute period and whether the hysteresis exceeds 200 mm
Hg.14 Education, competency assessment, and validation should be conducted before
using a pneumatic tourniquet, and documentation on the use of the tourniquet should
be included in the patient’s medical records. A pneumatic tourniquet should be applied
only by experienced personnel who are knowledgeable about its use and potential
complications.
In addition to physical maintenance of the tourniquet, patient-specific factors should be
considered before use of a tourniquet. Relative contraindications to tourniquet use
should be investigated before application and generally include peripheral vascular
disease, prosthetic vascular graft, severe infection or soft-tissue injury, poor cardiac
reserve, peripheral neuropathy, active venous thrombosis, Raynaud disease, and
occasionally sickle cell disease. In general, the use a tourniquet in patients with sickle cell
disease is safe if they are well oxygenated and their acid-base status is optimized
perioperatively.15
Proper Selection and Application
Cuff Positioning
Deflate and smooth before application.
Do not place directly over bony prominences.
Location on the limb should allow for adequate and potentially extensile surgical exposure.

Cuff Positioning
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:56 AM
AAOS | Tourniquets
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003021
9/33

In placing a tourniquet on a patient, the tourniquet cuff should be deflated and
smoothed before application. Traditionally, the cuff is carefully applied to the proximal
aspect of the limb at which the greatest circumference and muscle bulk is present,
theoretically affording the greatest protection against direct nerve injury.14 However, the
concept of selecting a proximal location has been refuted,16 noting that tourniquets
placed at the calf,17 ankle,18 forearm,19 and wrist20 are safe and effective. Researchers
assert that the muscle is not compressible10 and, therefore, cannot lower intraneural
pressure or protect the nerve. To avoid the risk of direct nerve compression, the cuff
should not be placed directly over bony prominences. For example, for a calf cuff, a
tourniquet should be at least 2 cm distal to the head of the fibula or 2 cm proximal to
the malleoli.
Cuff Size
The cuff is individualize based on the size and circumference of the patient’s limb.
At least 3 inches but no more than 6 inches of overlap should be present.
Cuff width should be the widest possible without encroaching on the surgical site.
Wider cuffs improve transmission of tissue compression and result in lower cuff pressures
required to compress the artery, minimizing pressure-related complications.

Cuff Size
Selecting the appropriate size tourniquet cuff is critical. The length of the cuff should be
individualized based on the size and circumference of the patient’s limb. The length of
the cuff should allow for at least 3 inches but no more than 6 inches of overlap because
this may generate higher pressures.21 The cuff should allow for a snug fit at the proximal
and distal edges, and the width should be the widest possible without encroaching on
the surgical site. The widest cuff possible should be used because wider cuffs improve
the transmission of tissue compression and result in lower cuff pressures required to
compress the artery, minimizing pressure-related complications.22 In a study on the
effect of cuff size on transmission of pressure to deeper tissues and on the elimination
of limb blood flow, Crenshaw et al23 measured tissue fluid pressure at four depths in

tissue compression at all tissue depths and transmit a greater percentage of the applied
tourniquet cuff pressure to deeper tissues (Figure 5); however, the tissue-fluid pressure
was always maximal at midcuff.

Underlying Limb Protection
Padding should protect the underlying skin to prevent wrinkles and blisters.
Multiple padding types have been used.
Prevent solutions from running under the tourniquet because this may lead to skin burns.

Underlying Limb Protection
Before the application of a tourniquet, staff must apply adequate padding under the
tourniquet with a soft dressing to prevent the wrinkles and blisters that may occur if the
skin is pinched. In a trial of 92 patients randomized to one of three groups, Olivecrona et
al25 confirmed an elastic stockinette under a pneumatic tourniquet cuff best protected
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:56 AM
AAOS | Tourniquets
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003021
13/33

against blisters during total knee arthroplasty. Multiple padding types have been used,
and surgeons should be familiar with the padding used in their operating theater. In a
study of 55 trials of five different types of limb protection beneath tourniquet cuffs on
the upper limbs and thighs of five adults, researchers found that stretched sleeves made
of two-layer tubular elastic material and matched to the specific tourniquet cuffs
produced considerably fewer, less severe pinches and wrinkles in the skin surface than
all other types of limb protection tested.22,26 Care should be taken to prevent solutions
from running under the tourniquet because this may lead to skin burns. Often, a
circumferential adhesive-backed plastic drape applied just distal to the tourniquet may
help prevent this.
Limb Exsanguination
Via direct limb elevation or by applying external compression
External compression is contraindicated in patients with infection and malignancy.

Limb Exsanguination
The limb may be exsanguinated before inflation of the tourniquet via direct limb
elevation or by applying external compression using a soft compression bandage from
distal to proximal. External compression in addition to elevation is thought to improve
the degree of limb exsanguination27 but is contraindicated in patients in whom infection
or a malignant lesion is suspected because this may force tumor cells or bacteria to the
proximal aspect of the extremity and into the bloodstream.28 The optimal timing and
angle of elevation for maximal exsanguination of the arm is 5 minutes at 90°.29 The
optimal timing and angle of elevation for maximal exsanguination of the leg is 5 minutes
at 45°.30 After exsanguination, tourniquet inflation should be rapid to prevent filling of
superficial veins before arterial occlusion.
Digital Tourniquet
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:56 AM
AAOS | Tourniquets
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003021
14/33

Safeguards of a pneumatic tourniquet are not available for most digital tourniquets.

Digital Tourniquet
Digital tourniquets in the form of a rolled glove, Penrose drain, or catheter generate a
wide and uncontrolled range of pressures and should be carefully used to prevent
severe complications.31 The safeguards of a pneumatic tourniquet generally are not
available for these devices; therefore, the surgeon must use them with extreme
vigilance. The National Patient Safety Agency has issued guidelines for the use of a digital
tourniquet, including the removal of digital tourniquets as part of the swab counting
procedure. The guidelines specify the need to record the length of time a tourniquet is in
place. They also suggest using digital tourniquets that are labeled and/or brightly
colored. The guidelines strongly recommend that surgical gloves should not be used as
tourniquets. Finally, the guidelines recommend that the World Health Organization
Surgical Safety Checklist should be reviewed, and tourniquet removal should be added
to the sign out stage of surgery.
Safe Pressure and Duration
Tourniquet complications increase as tourniquet time increases.
A safe time limit of 1 to 3 hours has been described and likely depends on occlusion pressure
and patient comorbidities.
If more than 2 hours are required, a tourniquet downtime technique may be used, and the
suggested reperfusion time between successive ischemic periods ranges from 3 to 20 minutes.

Safe Pressure and Duration
Tourniquet-related complications increase as tourniquet time increases.32-34 A safe
duration and pressure for tourniquet use remains controversial, and no strict guidelines
have been established; however, minimizing tourniquet time to minimize the risk of
injury is a commonly accepted strategy. The pressure at which a tourniquet should be
inflated depends on the size and shape of the extremity and the patient’s blood
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:56 AM
AAOS | Tourniquets
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003021
15/33

pressure. Multiple methods to determine pneumatic tourniquet inflation pressure have
been used. One strategy involves adding 50 to 75 mm Hg to the pressure required to
obliterate the peripheral pulse and compensate for collateral circulation and blood
pressure changes.35 Another strategy involves adding 90 to 100 mm Hg to the
preoperative systolic arm blood pressure for lower limb surgery.36
Limb Occlusion Pressure
Lowest pressure that maintains a bloodless surgical field
LOP is the minimum pressure required to stop the flow of arterial blood distal to the cuff.
Target pressures based on the LOP include a safety margin to account for physiologic
intraoperative variations in arterial pressure.
If the LOP is less than 130 mm Hg, the safety margin is 40 mm Hg.
If the LOP is 131 to 190 mm Hg, the safety margin is 60 mm Hg.
If LOP is greater than 190 mm Hg, the safety margin is 80 mm Hg.
For pediatric patients, adding 50 mm Hg is recommended.

Limb Occlusion Pressure
The tourniquet inflation pressure should be maintained at the lowest pressure that
maintains a bloodless surgical field.9 LOP is defined as the minimum pressure required,
at a specific time by a specific tourniquet cuff applied to a specific patient’s limb at a
specific location, to stop the flow of arterial blood into the limb distal to the cuff.3 Cuff
pressures based on LOP measured immediately preoperatively generally are lower than
commonly used pressures and are sufficient in maintaining a satisfactorily bloodless
surgical field. LOP inherently accounts for variables such as systolic blood pressure,
tourniquet cuff design, cuff application method, limb circumference and shape, and
tissue characteristics at the cuff site. Setting tourniquet pressure based on LOP
minimizes the pressure and pressure gradients applied by a cuff to an underlying limb
and helps minimize the risk of nerve-related injuries. The Association of Perioperative
Registered Nurses has issued guidelines for target pressures based on the LOP, with a
safety margin added to account for physiologic intraoperative variations in arterial
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:56 AM
AAOS | Tourniquets
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003021
16/33

pressure.37 If the LOP is less than 130 mm Hg, the safety margin is 40 mm Hg. If the LOP
is 131 to 190 mm Hg, the safety margin is 60 mm Hg. If the LOP is greater than 190 mm
Hg, the safety margin is 80 mm Hg. Finally, for pediatric patients, adding 50 mm Hg is
recommended.26
Duration of Tourniquet Use
Safe time limit depends on occlusion pressure and patient comorbidities.
A duration of 2 hours is considered safe for upper-limb surgery.
Dose-response with nerve injury
Prolonged use is associated with a threefold increase in neurologic complications for each
additional 30 minutes of inflation.
Tourniquet downtime technique beyond prescribed time
The tourniquet is released for a short period before reinflation.

Duration of Tourniquet Use
A safe tourniquet time limit of 1 to 3 hours has been described and likely depends on
occlusion pressure and patient comorbidities.38,39 Although no prospective randomized
clinical trials have defined the optimal duration of tourniquet use in the lower limb, 2
hours is considered relatively safe for upper-limb surgery.14 Depending on cuff inflation
pressure, greater muscle injury is induced beneath the tourniquet than distal to the
tourniquet, with a topographic pattern of necrosis observed after 2 hours of tourniquet
compression. Therefore, 2 hours of tourniquet use generally is considered safe for
human upper-limb surgery.32,40 The duration of uninterrupted tourniquet inflation
increases the risk of neural dysfunction postoperatively. A dose-response with nerve
injury exist because prolonged use is associated with an almost threefold increase in
neurologic complications for each additional 30 minutes of inflation.41 One method to
avoid ischemic injury to muscle cells may involve a tourniquet downtime technique, in
which the tourniquet is released for a short period before reinflation. Although evidence
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:56 AM
AAOS | Tourniquets
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003021
17/33

to support this technique is limited, if more than 2 hours is required, the suggested
reperfusion time between successive ischemic periods ranges from 3 to 20 minutes.42,43
Physiologic Effects Associated with Tourniquets
Effects of Exsanguination
Clears the surgical field
Reduces overall blood loss
Reduces the risk of microemboli at time of tourniquet release.
Autotransfusion from peripheral to central circulation

Effects of Exsanguination
In many patients, the surgical limb is exsanguinated via elevation and/or a compressive
bandage. However, this is not the case in musculoskeletal cancer surgery, and the limb
should not be forcefully exsanguinated because it may force tumor cells to the proximal
aspect of the extremity and into the bloodstream.28 The advantages of emptying the
blood vessels from the distal end to the proximal end before tourniquet inflation include
establishing a clear surgical field, reducing overall blood loss, and reducing the risk of
microemboli at the time of tourniquet release. In addition, the exsanguination results in
an autotransfusion of blood from the peripheral circulation to the central circulation.
Effects of Use and Pain
Progressive hypoxia, acidosis, and cooling of extremity
Increased capillary permeability causes interstitial edema.
Cellular pH and pO2 decrease with a concurrent increase in pCO2, potassium, and lactate.
Muscle is most susceptible to ischemic injury, and creatine phosphokinase levels elevate after
1.5 hours.
Arterial hypertension and tourniquet pain occur in as many as two-thirds of patients after 30
and 60 minutes of inflation.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:56 AM
AAOS | Tourniquets
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003021
18/33


Effects of Use and Pain
Multiple cellular and systemic effects result from tourniquet inflation. With the
tourniquet inflated, progressive hypoxia, acidosis, and cooling of the occluded extremity
occurs on the cellular level.43 This is associated with increased capillary permeability44
and coagulation changes.45 At 30 to 60 minutes after tourniquet inflation, histologic
evidence of muscle damage is observed. With depletion of high-energy phosphate,
subsequent loss of physiologic ion gradients across cell membranes occurs because of
impaired sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase activity.46 Beyond 60 minutes of
inflation, interstitial edema develops.43 Over time, the cellular pH decreases, with a
concurrent increase in pCO2, potassium, and lactate, and a decrease in pO2.47 In canine
models, 3 hours of sustained tourniquet ischemia results in widespread, reversible injury
to skeletal myocytes.42 Muscle is more susceptible to ischemic injury than other tissues
in the extremity, and limiting tourniquet application to 1.5 hours avoids elevations in
serum creatine phosphokinase levels.42,48
Systemic effects of tourniquet inflation include tourniquet-induced arterial hypertension
and tourniquet pain, which occurs in as many as two-thirds of patients and has an onset
between 30 and 60 minutes after inflation. Hypertension is believed to occur because of
tissue ischemia, eliciting a neural mediated cardiovascular response by a generalized
sympathetic pressor reflex.49,50 An increase in central venous pressure also occurs
during tourniquet inflation, which may alter patient hemodynamics. Tourniquet pain
develops in as many as two-thirds of patients after 30 to 60 minutes of cuff inflation.
Tourniquet pain consists of several components and is not caused only by pain from the
pressure under the tourniquet.51 Multiple strategies have been used to reduce
tourniquet pain, including eutectic mixture of local anesthetic cream application;52 local
anesthetic via neuraxial anesthesia with or without opioids;53,54 intravenous regional
anesthesia;55,56 magnesium sulfate;57 ketamine;58 ketorolac, dexmetomidine, and
clonidine;59,60 electroacupuncture; and meditation.61 Surgeons should discuss
tourniquet pain with their anesthesia provider and work together to reduce its effect on
patient outcomes. In addition, patients should be continuously monitored with special
consideration of parameters such as hypertension and tachycardia as surrogate markers

Effects of Reperfusion After Deflation
Reperfusion restores energy supplies and removes toxic metabolites.
Ischemia during inflation primes tissue for injury during reperfusion.
Systemic effects
Return of toxic metabolites to systemic circulation results in myonephropathic metabolic
syndrome.
Metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, myoglobinemia, and myoglobinuria
Myoglobinuria may induce acute renal failure, additional metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia,
and even death.
Reactive hyperemia causes as much as a 10% increase in limb size, resulting in swelling and
stiffness.
Cellular effects
Ischemic damage mediated by oxygen-free radicals, nitric oxide, cytokines, and arachidonic
acid metabolites.
Results in necrosis and mitochondrial dysfunction

Effects of Reperfusion After Deflation
The tourniquet must come down at some point; although reperfusion is obligatory in
restoring energy supplies and removing toxic metabolites, ischemia during tourniquet
inflation primes tissue for additional injury that occurs during reperfusion. Loss of ion
gradients across the cellular membrane of ischemic myocytes results in leakage of
potassium ions into the interstitium.46 Reactive hyperemia after tourniquet deflation
causes as much as a 10% increase in limb size, resulting in swelling and stiffness.14 In
addition, release of intracellular enzymes (creatine phosphokinase, lactic acid
dehydrogenase, and glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase) and myoglobin occurs as a part
of this rhabdomyolysis. The return of these toxic metabolites to systemic circulation
results in myonephropathic metabolic syndrome,62 characterized by metabolic acidosis,

hyperkalemia, myoglobinemia, and myoglobinuria. The precipitation of myoglobin in the
collecting tubules of the kidneys may induce acute renal failure and additional metabolic
acidosis, which may result in hyperkalemia and even death. Tourniquet deflation also
leads to a decrease in mean arterial blood pressure, partly from a decrease in systemic
peripheral vascular resistance and partly from the release of metabolites from the
ischemic limb, which decreases the compliance of vessels. This often manifests as an
increase in end-tidal CO2, a decrease in core temperature, and a decrease in central
venous oxygen tension. In the setting of intramedullary instrumentation, cementation,
or insertion of a prosthesis in the lower limb, deflation of a pneumatic tourniquet is
associated with an increased risk of a sudden release of venous emboli, possibly
resulting in right heart strain and emphasizing the need for careful patient monitoring at
that time.63 Simultaneous deflation of tourniquets should be avoided if bilateral
simultaneous total knee arthroplasty is performed during a single anesthetic event to
reduce the risk of severe hemodynamic fluctuations. Tourniquet deflation is
paradoxically associated with thrombolytic activity because anoxia promotes activation
of the antithrombin III and protein C pathways, which has been implicated in post-
tourniquet bleeding.3
In addition to the systemic effects that occur after tourniquet deflation, the return of
circulation to the limb may lead to reperfusion injury,64 which is characterized by
necrosis and mitochondrial dysfunction.65 Reperfusion injury represents a paradoxical
extension of ischemic damage mediated by oxygen-free radicals and nitric oxide,
cytokines, and arachidonic acid metabolites. L-arginine management may limit the
extent of injury;66 however, clinical studies to support the widespread of L-arginine are
lacking.

Nerve Injury
Nerve injury is the most common serious complication of tourniquet use and ranges
from mild, transient loss of function to irreversible damage and paralysis. The
pathophysiology of tourniquet-induced nerve injury likely is a combination of mechanical
compression and neural ischemia.41 Most nerve injuries are limited to the portion of the
nerve beneath and near the edges of the cuff, resulting from compressive neurapraxia
rather than ischemic neuropathy.70-72 Compression of large myelinated fibers involves
displacement of the node of Ranvier from its usual position under the Schwann-cell
junction (Figure 7) accompanied by stretching of the paranodal myelin on one side of
the node and invagination of the paranodal myelin on the side of the node. Nodal
displacement of as much as 300 μm from its original position results in partial or
complete rupture of the stretched paranodal myelin. Maximal nodal displacement
occurs under the edges of the cuff, the location at which the applied pressure gradient is
greatest. Relative or complete sparring of the nodes is observed directly under the
center of the cuff.

function and delayed recovery, suggesting tourniquet-induced neuropathy is causal in
impaired rehabilitation.77
Delayed Recovery of Muscle Power and Postoperative Mobilization
Demonstrable delay in recovery of straight leg-raising power after knee surgery
performed with the use of a tourniquet78 results in prolonged rehabilitation and the
potential for falls.

Intraoperative Bleeding
Bleeding can occur, even if a tourniquet is applied to a limb; this may be attributed to
an underpressurized cuff, insufficient exsanguination, improper cuff selection, a
loosely applied cuff, calcified vessels, or elongated inflation or deflation.79

Systemic Complications
Arterial Embolization
Consideration should be given to surgical treatment performed without a tourniquet in
patients with severe peripheral vascular disease. 
Preoperative consultation with vascular surgery is recommended for these patients.86,87
Pulmonary and Venous Embolization
Massive pulmonary embolism has been reported during tourniquet inflation in patients with
deep vein thrombosis; therefore, care should be taken during exsanguination.88
Venous embolization, particularly in the lower limb, also has been reported after tourniquet
deflation.89

Complication Prevention
Pearls and measures to avoid complications with the use of a pneumatic tourniquet include
the following:14
Higher levels of tourniquet pressure and higher pressure gradients under tourniquet cuffs
are associated with a higher risk of nerve-related injury.
Measurement of LOP may help to minimize tourniquet pressure levels and pressure
gradients.
Selective use of pneumatic, wider, and contoured tourniquet cuffs reduces tourniquet
pressure levels and the applied pressure gradients.
Avoid exceeding tourniquet ischemia times beyond 2 hours.
Ensure good padding beneath the tourniquet, and do not allow any solution applied to the
skin to run beneath the tourniquet.
Carefully monitor the perioperative hemodynamic status of patients with poor
cardiopulmonary reserve.
Summary

Summary
Modern pneumatic tourniquets, if used properly, aid in extremity surgery by decreasing
intraoperative blood loss and providing a relatively bloodless field. Tourniquets are
designed to minimize the incidence of complications, and prospective, randomized
clinical trials have demonstrated no substantial long-term negative effects associated
with their use during extremity surgery.92,93 Safe tourniquet use requires using proper
padding, not exceeding the safe limit of tourniquet pressure and duration, and deflating

pathophysiology of tourniquet-induced skeletal muscle ischemia-reperfusion injury, and
the potential pitfalls associated with the use of pneumatic tourniquets.
